title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
description: Brute force to optimized: iteratively expanding a combination list versus a direct backtracking recursion, one digit at a time.

sections.title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number

content.title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a string digits containing digits from 2 to 9, return all possible letter combinations that the number could represent, using the standard telephone keypad mapping (2=abc, 3=def, 4=ghi, 5=jkl, 6=mno, 7=pqrs, 8=tuv, 9=wxyz). Return the combinations in any order.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","digits, a string of digits 2 through 9"],["Output","All possible letter combinations the digits could represent"],["Goal","Generate every combination by choosing one letter per digit"],["Constraints","0 <= digits.length <= 4"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Every possible combination by picking one option per position\"","Backtracking: build a partial combination digit by digit, recursing and undoing"],["A fixed mapping of choices per position (each digit maps to 3 or 4 letters)","A simple recursive tree with a small, bounded branching factor"]]}

blocks.text: For each digit in the input, there is a fixed small set of possible letters (3 or 4 depending on the digit). A valid combination picks exactly one letter for each digit position, in order. All such combinations, across every digit, need to be returned.

blocks.title: Analogy: Old Phone Text Messages
blocks.text: Picture typing a text message on an old numeric keypad phone, where pressing "2" could mean "a", "b", or "c". For a given digit sequence, this problem asks for every possible word/combination of letters that pressing those digits (choosing one letter each time) could produce.

blocks.caption: Each digit branches into its possible letters, building combinations one digit at a time

blocks.text: Result: ["ad", "ae", "af", "bd", "be", "bf", "cd", "ce", "cf"]. Digit 2 maps to a,b,c and digit 3 maps to d,e,f, giving all 9 combinations.

Before generating anything, notice this is a "choose one option per position, try every combination" problem, the signature of backtracking: build a partial answer, recurse to the next position, and let the recursion naturally explore every branch.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Each digit position independently offers 3 or 4 letter choices, and a full combination requires picking exactly one letter at every position.

Observation 2: This naturally forms a recursive structure: at each digit position, try every possible letter for that digit, and for each choice, recurse into the next position with the choice appended.

Observation 3: The base case is reaching the end of the digits string, at which point the currently built combination is complete and should be recorded.

Observation 4: Since digits.length is at most 4, and each digit contributes at most 4 choices, the total number of combinations is at most 4^4 = 256, so a direct backtracking approach is efficient enough.

This leads to a straightforward backtracking function: at digit index i, try every letter mapped to digits[i], append it, recurse to i+1, and once i equals the length of digits, record the built-up combination.
An alternative to recursion is iterative list expansion: start with an empty combination, and for each digit, expand every existing partial combination by appending each of that digit's letters.

items: Start with a list containing just the empty string.
For each digit, build a new list by taking every existing partial string and appending each possible letter for that digit.
Replace the old list with the new, expanded list.
After processing all digits, the list contains every combination.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Iteratively expanding the combination list avoids explicit recursion, but it builds and discards many intermediate string lists.
This works fine given the small constraints, but is less direct than building combinations digit by digit through recursion.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(4^n times n), where n is digits.length (up to 4 letters per digit, plus O(n) string copying per combination).
Space: O(4^n times n) for storing all intermediate and final combinations.

Limitation: not really a limitation for this problem's tiny constraints, but recursion (backtracking) more directly matches the structure of the problem and avoids building intermediate lists at every step.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Since the constraints are tiny (at most 4 digits), "optimizing" here is really about choosing the most natural and direct technique, backtracking, rather than iteratively expanding lists.

Backtracking builds one combination at a time: at each digit position, try each possible letter, append it to the current partial combination, recurse into the next position, and once all digits are used, record the combination directly, without needing to build or copy full lists at every level.

Because a string (or a character array with a pointer) is passed down through recursion, there is no need for the expand-and-discard list pattern.

Use backtracking: at digit index i, for every letter mapped to digits[i], append it to the current combination and recurse to i+1. Once i reaches digits.length, add the completed combination to the answer.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Path","Result"],"rows":[["digit 2 -> a, digit 3 -> d","\"ad\""],["digit 2 -> a, digit 3 -> e","\"ae\""],["digit 2 -> b, digit 3 -> d","\"bd\""],["... (continues for all 3x3=9 combinations)","..."]]}

blocks.caption: Backtrack digit by digit, trying each letter, recursing, and recording complete combinations

blocks.text: Backtracking directly mirrors the problem structure: choosing one letter for the current digit, recursing to handle the remaining digits, and undoing the choice before trying the next letter (in languages using a mutable buffer) explores every combination exactly once, in a natural depth-first order, without ever building or discarding intermediate lists.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(4^n times n), where n is digits.length, generating each of up to 4^n combinations and spending O(n) to build/copy each one.
Space: O(n) for the recursion depth and current buffer, plus O(4^n times n) for the output.

blocks.text: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number is a foundational backtracking problem: one choice per position, from a small fixed set of options, explored via recursion with a natural base case.

items: Forgetting to return an empty list (not a list containing an empty string) when digits is empty.
Mismapping digit "7" (4 letters: pqrs) or "9" (4 letters: wxyz), which have 4 letters instead of the usual 3.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["digits is empty","Return an empty list, not [\"\"]."],["digits has a single character","Return each of that digit's letters as a single-character combination."]]}

blocks.text: Stating clearly upfront "this is a backtracking problem: one choice per position, recurse, base case at the end" before writing any code demonstrates pattern recognition clearly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "generate every combination from a fixed set of choices per position", think: backtracking, one recursive call per choice, base case at the final position.

items: How would you generate the combinations lazily (as a generator/iterator) instead of building the full list upfront?
How would you extend this to support a custom keypad mapping?
Permutations, Subsets, Combination Sum, all classic backtracking problems with the same "choose, recurse, undo" template.
Generate Parentheses, another small fixed-choice backtracking problem.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both the iterative expansion and the backtracking approach run in O(4^n times n) time; backtracking uses only O(n) extra space beyond the output, making it the more natural and efficient choice.

items: Pattern: backtracking, one choice per position from a small fixed set, recurse, base case at the end.
Core Idea: at each digit, try every mapped letter, append it, recurse into the next digit, and record complete combinations once all digits are used.
Time: O(4^n times n) for both approaches.
Space: O(4^n times n) for the list-expansion approach, O(n) recursion depth for backtracking (excluding output).
Most Important Observation: a fixed small set of choices per position is the classic signature of backtracking.
Interview Difficulty: an accessible, foundational backtracking problem, often used to introduce the pattern.
One line memory trick: pick a letter, recurse to the next digit, undo, repeat.
